does: Cuts food into even cubes, so that every piece cooks at the same speed.

intro.what: Dicing cuts food into even cubes.
intro.why: Even pieces cook at a similar pace, so the cut helps you control texture as well as appearance.

how: Trim the piece so that it has a flat side and sits still on the board.
Cut it into slabs as thick as the cube you want.
Stack the slabs and cut them into sticks of the same width.
Turn the sticks and cut across them into cubes.
For an onion, halve it through the root, cut towards the root without cutting through it, then slice across.

cues.text: The cubes are all one size, with square edges.
The knife glides forward and down. Your knuckles guide the blade and your fingertips stay tucked behind them.

mistakes.mistake: Pieces of different sizes, so the small ones turn to mush before the large ones are tender.
mistakes.fix: Set the thickness with the first cut. Every later cut copies it.

mistakes.mistake: Chasing a round vegetable that rolls under the knife.
mistakes.fix: Cut a thin slice off one side first and rest it on that flat.

quiz.question: Why aim for even cubes when dicing?
choices: So the outside of every piece browns before any centre softens.
So the pieces cook at a similar pace.
So stirring becomes unnecessary during cooking.
quiz.because: Even-sized pieces cook at a similar pace, so small pieces do not soften long before larger ones.

quiz.question: What sequence makes cubes after you have a flat, stable piece?
choices: Cut slabs of different thicknesses, then chop the pile together.
Slice across a rounded piece without trimming.
Cut slabs, then sticks, then across the sticks.
quiz.because: Slabs become sticks, then cubes. Matching the thickness at each stage keeps the final pieces even.

quiz.question: What should the finished pile look like?
choices: Cubes of a similar size with square edges.
A mixture of thin shards and large chunks.
quiz.because: Similar-sized cubes with square edges show that the cuts stayed consistent.

quiz.question: A round vegetable rolls as you try to cut it. What should you change first?
choices: Hold it more firmly on its rounded side and continue slicing.
Trim a flat side and rest it on that side.
Start with curved slices while it rests on its round side.
quiz.because: A flat resting side keeps the vegetable from rolling while you cut.

comes_after.why: A dice is a slice cut again, lengthwise and across, so an even slice comes first.
